I think it's actually quite important, and maybe underappreciated from the outside. People tend to see Sam as the business and fundraising person and Greg as the engineer, and that's roughly true, but what matters more is that both of them stay close enough to the technical work that they can make real calls about it.

Greg especially is very hands-on. He's someone who will just sit down and write code, debug infrastructure, look at training runs. When a leader does that, it sends a strong signal: engineering quality matters here, and nobody is too senior to care about details. It also means that when there's a disagreement about direction, there's someone at the top who can understand the tradeoffs at a fairly low level instead of just hearing summaries.

Sam's role is a bit different. He's less about the code and more about setting priorities and making sure the company bets on a few big things instead of spreading itself thin. In a place full of very smart researchers, everyone has their own idea of what's most interesting, so you need someone who says, "OK, this is the direction, let's put compute and people behind it." That kind of focus is a big part of why things like scaling up GPT models, or shipping ChatGPT, could happen as fast as they did.

That said, I don't want to overstate it. A lot of the technical alignment comes from the culture and from people in the middle: the researchers and engineers who coordinate with each other, share infrastructure, and agree on what good work looks like. Leadership can set the tone and make the big bets, but they can't personally keep hundreds of people aligned. What they can do is hire people who care about the same things and keep the bar high. I think that's really the main way they keep the company together technically.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, from where I sat as an engineer, the thing that struck me most about Sam and Greg is that they're very different, and that difference is kind of the point.

Greg is still deeply technical. He'll actually be in the codebase. There were stretches where he'd be debugging training infrastructure late at night alongside the team, not as a symbolic gesture but because he genuinely wanted to understand where things were breaking. When your president can read your pull request and ask a sharp question about it, that changes the culture. People don't hand-wave. You can't tell him "the model is just behaving weirdly," because he'll ask you which layer, which data mix, what changed in the run.

Sam operates at a different altitude. He's less about the specific engineering decisions and more about setting the direction and making sure resources flow to the right bets. Compute allocation, which projects get prioritized, what the company is actually trying to accomplish in the next year. That sounds abstract, but in a place like OpenAI it's incredibly concrete, because compute is the scarcest thing you have, and whoever decides how it gets split is shaping the technical agenda whether they write code or not.

So when you ask about keeping the company technically aligned, I'd say it works through two channels. One is Greg keeping the leadership honest about what's really happening on the ground. The other is Sam making sure the dozens of teams, all of whom have strong opinions about what matters, are pulling toward something coherent rather than each building their own island.

That said, I don't want to oversell it. A company that size doesn't stay aligned because two people will it to be. Most of the real alignment comes from the researchers and engineers in the middle, the people leading individual efforts who talk to each other constantly. Leadership sets the frame, but if the frame doesn't match what the people running experiments are seeing, it falls apart fast. The times things worked best were when there was a tight loop between the two, and the times it was harder were when the vision got ahead of what the infrastructure or the research could actually support.

Alignment doesn’t mean everyone agrees all the time; it means people understand the direction and can challenge it when the evidence points somewhere else.
